name: Jawline filler
lead: Jawline filler is the injection of a dermal filler, most often a hyaluronic acid (HA) or calcium hydroxylapatite (CaHA) product, along the mandible to add definition or volume to the jaw angle, jawline or chin area. It is a non-surgical option used to accentuate a sharper or wider lower face, to address a jawline contour deficit, and to reduce the look of jowls.[2][3][11] Because most fillers are gradually absorbed, the look is adjustable and is maintained with repeat sessions.[11][13]

Registered clinical studies have examined fillers for jawline contouring, including a 180-participant study of a CaHA product, HA products from several manufacturers, and a study of filler in jowls.[3][4][5][6][7][8] A 2026 review in Dermatologic Surgery groups jawline filler with temple, nose and lip treatment as high-impact but higher-risk areas, with possible complications ranging from contour irregularities to tissue necrosis, vision loss and embolic events.[2]

In looksmaxxing communities, jawline filler is discussed as a reversible or lower-commitment alternative to jaw implants, and users on looksmax.org share before-and-after impressions, polls and maintenance-cost estimates.[9][10] Research on aesthetic-surgery interest finds that cosmetic procedure interest among men has changed over recent decades, which authors link to declining stigma.[1] The US FDA classes dermal fillers as prescription medical devices and advises that they be injected by licensed, trained providers rather than self-administered.[14]

paras: Filler is injected by a clinician along or near the mandibular border to add projection or straighten a perceived contour deficit. HA fillers are made of cross-linked hyaluronic acid, which the body gradually breaks down, while CaHA products are used for firmer volume.[11] Fillers are regulated as medical devices in the United States and require a CE mark in the UK and EEA.[11]

HA is a polysaccharide that combines with water and swells into a gel, and most HA fillers are cross-linked, commonly with BDDE, to extend how long they last.[11][13] HA was first isolated from bovine vitreous by Karl Meyer and John Palmer in 1934; the first hyaluronan biomedical product, Healon, was developed by Pharmacia for eye surgery rather than as a filler.[13] Wide use of dermal fillers began in the 1980s.[11]

Published reviews of high-risk facial areas discuss anatomy, product selection, injection technique, clinical benefits and complication-mitigation strategies for the jawline alongside the temple, nose and lip.[2]

HA fillers are the most common and are valued for biocompatibility and biodegradability.[11] CaHA products such as the one in the 180-participant jawline study provide firmer volume.[3][11] Other filler materials described in the literature include poly-L-lactic acid, which stimulates collagen production, and PMMA, which relies on particles that induce fibrous tissue.[11] The FDA notes that no dermal fillers are approved for over-the-counter use and that injectable silicone is not approved for any aesthetic use.[14]

A 2024 case report described treating the double chin (submental fullness) with HA injection.[15] Chin filler is studied alongside the jawline: a phase 4 study of filler for chin profile enhancement in chin regression, asymmetry and jawline contour deficit is registered.[8] Filler in the jowls has its own registered study.[7]

sections.h: How it is used for appearance
paras: Jawline filler is used to build a more defined or wider lower third of the face: adding volume at the gonial angle, along the border and at the chin changes the contour seen from the front and in profile, and can make the transition from neck to jaw look sharper. Clinicians also place filler to address jowls, where the aim is a straighter line along the jaw.[7][11]

Looksmaxxing posters describe it as a way to preview how a more defined jaw looks, and as a lower-commitment option than implants because HA filler fades and can be dissolved.[9][10][13] Some forum users describe it as a stepping stone before planned surgery such as implants or rhinoplasty.[10][12]

Registered interventional studies include a completed 180-participant study of a CaHA product to improve jawline contour by adding volume (NCT03583359), completed studies of HA products for jawline contour deficit or jaw volume deficit including a 40-participant study (NCT06336759), a 114-participant post-market follow-up of Decoria Intense Strong (NCT06562075) and a 72-participant study of YVOIRE Y-Solution 720 (NCT04886544).[3][4][5][6]

A 16-participant study examined filler for jowl improvement (NCT04389866), and a phase 4 study of filler for chin profile enhancement in chin regression, asymmetry and jawline contour deficit is recruiting (NCT07777926).[7][8] The published literature identified consists mostly of device registrations and safety-oriented reviews rather than long-term randomized comparisons against surgery, and no results from the registered studies were identified.
Documented harms specific to the area include a case report of vascular occlusion of the sublingual artery after jawline filler injection.[12]

A 2026 review lists risks for filler in high-impact facial regions ranging from contour irregularities to tissue necrosis, vision loss and embolic events.[2] Wikipedia describes common filler effects as bruising, redness, pain and itching, with infection, allergic reactions and lumps less often, and blindness from retrograde embolization rare but usually permanent.[11]

The FDA names unintentional injection into a blood vessel as the most serious risk, with possible tissue death, vision problems and stroke that may be permanent. It lists swelling, tenderness, rash, nodules, infection, migration and, rarely, anaphylaxis, and notes that removing filler may be difficult or impossible, especially for permanent fillers or those not made of HA.[14] The agency recommends licensed providers with dermatology or plastic-surgery experience, advises against self-injection and buying fillers online because products may be counterfeit or unapproved, and issued warnings about counterfeit fillers in 2017 and 2018.[14]

In the jaw region, a case report described occlusion of the sublingual artery, a vessel in the floor of the mouth, after jawline injection.[12] Wikipedia notes that exercise and strenuous activity can increase blood flow and shorten filler lifespan.[11]

On looksmax.org, users post accounts of jawline filler results, including one thread in which the original poster described the effect seen one week after swelling had resolved and invited a poll on the outcome.[9] Another user described a filler programme for the gonial angle and chin as a step toward feeling comfortable with their appearance, estimated an ongoing cost of about 1,000 to 2,000 US dollars per year for maintenance, and named jaw implants as an eventual goal, a choice other users questioned.[10]

Other threads include a poster asking whether others noticed a changed jawline after filler, a thread titled around a filler 'transformation', a request for ratings of a result, a thread on a 'crazy' jaw-filler ascension, and a post about dissolving jaw filler.[16][17][18][19][20] One poster shared a plan that combined jaw and lip filler with rhinoplasty and described doing the filler themselves; the FDA advises against self-injection.[21][14]
Commenters in these threads share advice that filler can be dissolved if unwanted, and one reply attributed a cheekbone look to skin being stretched by filler.[9][10]

lore.intro: Jawline filler is discussed on looksmax.org as a non-surgical way to add jaw definition, often as a stepping stone before or instead of implants, with posters sharing result photos, polls and cost estimates.[9][10]

claims.claim: Jawline filler gives a visible sharper jaw once swelling settles
claims.believers: One original poster showed the effect a week after treatment, after swelling had gone down, and asked others to vote on the result.[9]
claims.experts: Registered studies have assessed filler for jawline contour deficit, but no results from them were identified; the clinical literature mainly discusses technique and risks.[3][4][2]

claims.claim: Filler is a worthwhile ongoing investment compared with surgery
claims.believers: A poster described spending roughly 1,000 to 2,000 US dollars a year on maintenance and called it an investment rather than a waste, while saving for implants.[10]
claims.experts: No published studies comparing the long-term cost or satisfaction of filler maintenance with implants were identified.[2]

claims.claim: Filler can be dissolved if unwanted
claims.believers: A reply in one thread advised that filler would not leave on its own and needed to be dissolved.[10]
claims.experts: General dermal-filler literature describes hyaluronic acid products as degradable over time, while other materials behave differently.[11]

claims.claim: Filler is a reversible trial run for a stronger jaw.
claims.believers: Posters describe filler as a way to see how a more defined jaw looks before committing to implants, and note it can be dissolved.[10][20]
claims.experts: HA fillers can be degraded by hyaluronidase enzymes, whereas the FDA notes removal may be difficult or impossible for permanent fillers and those not made of HA.[13][14]

claims.claim: Filler gives a result visible once swelling settles.
claims.believers: A poster showed a one-week result after swelling and asked for votes.[9]
claims.experts: Registered studies assess jawline contour deficit as an outcome, though no results from them were identified.[3][4][5]

claims.claim: Doing jaw filler yourself is a workable route.
claims.believers: One poster described a plan to inject jaw filler themselves and to document it.[21]
claims.experts: The FDA advises against self-injection and buying fillers online, citing counterfeit products and the risk of blood-vessel injection.[14]

claims.claim: Filler in the jaw area is low risk.
claims.believers: Forum threads discuss results and costs and rarely focus on complications.[9][10]
claims.experts: A 2026 review lists contour irregularities, necrosis, vision loss and embolic events as possible complications in high-risk areas including the jawline, and a case report describes sublingual artery occlusion.[2][12]

claims.claim: Stretched skin from filler can improve nearby features such as the cheekbones.
claims.believers: A reply in a result thread attributed a strong cheekbone look to filler stretching the skin.[9]
claims.experts: No published study identified examines remote effects of jawline filler on cheek appearance.

card.summary: Hyaluronic acid or CaHA injected along the mandible to sharpen the jawline without surgery; trials are registered but risks include rare vascular events.
card.aka: Jaw filler, jawline contouring, gonial angle filler
card.note: Filler in the lower face carries rare vascular complications; effects are temporary and need repeat treatment.

quick.overview:
Jawline filler is a non-surgical treatment in which a clinician places a dermal filler, typically HA or CaHA, along the jaw to add definition or volume. It is often discussed as an alternative to jaw implants.

Several device studies for jawline contouring are registered, but the published literature mainly covers technique and risk.
quick.mechanism: The gel adds volume under the skin along the mandibular angle and border, changing the contour. It is gradually absorbed, so effects fade and repeat sessions are needed.
quick.risks: Common effects are swelling, bruising and pain. Reviews describe rarer events including contour irregularities, tissue necrosis, vascular occlusion and, in other facial areas, vision loss. A 2026 case report described occlusion of the sublingual artery after jawline filler. Fillers are regulated as medical devices.
